title: Metrics and the north star
summary: Pick the one number that shows users are getting value, and the numbers that move it.

lessons.title: What a north star metric is
teach: A north star metric is the one number that best shows users are getting real value. If it goes up, the product is helping more people.
Revenue is usually a bad north star. It can rise while users get less value, for example by adding hidden fees.

questions.prompt: Which is the best north star for Zepto?
options: Orders delivered on time and complete each week
questions.explain: It counts value the customer actually felt: the right items, fast. Revenue and downloads can grow while customers get a worse experience.

questions.prompt: A good north star should be something a product team can influence.
questions.explain: If no team can move it, it can't guide decisions. Spotify's time spent listening is moved by better recommendations.

questions.prompt: Match each product to a sensible north star.
questions.explain: Each one counts the moment the user gets value: a stay, a day of learning, a team talking.

questions.prompt: Put these steps for choosing a north star in order.
steps: Write down the core value users get
List numbers that capture that value
Check the team can move it week to week
Add guardrail metrics so it can't be gamed
questions.explain: Start from user value, then find a number, then test that it is useful and safe.

questions.prompt: Pick the 3 numbers that directly drive weekly orders on a quick delivery app.
questions.explain: Weekly orders = buyers x orders per buyer x success rate. Staff and ratings matter but are not direct parts of the formula.

questions.prompt: One of these north star choices is weak. Which one?
questions.explain: Discounts are a cost, not user value. More discounts can mean a weaker business, not happier users.

questions.prompt: What is a guardrail metric?
options: A number that must not get worse while you chase the goal
A metric only finance looks at
questions.explain: If Blinkit pushes faster delivery, a guardrail like order accuracy makes sure speed doesn't break quality.

lessons.title: Good metrics and vanity metrics
teach: A vanity metric looks good but does not help you decide anything. Total downloads only goes up, even if everyone has stopped using the app.
A good metric changes when the product gets better or worse, and it points to an action.
Rates and ratios are often better than totals: share of users who come back, orders per user, time to deliver.

questions.prompt: Which is a vanity metric?
options: Share of new users still active after 30 days
Orders per active user per week
Share of orders delivered on time
questions.explain: Total downloads can only rise. It says nothing about whether people still use the app.

questions.prompt: A good metric should help you decide what to do next.
questions.explain: If 'week 1 return rate' drops, you know to look at the first week experience. That's an action.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a vanity metric for Spotify?
lines: Share of free users who become paid
questions.explain: A huge catalogue sounds nice, but it doesn't show listeners are happy. The other three track real behaviour.

questions.prompt: Swap each vanity metric for a better one.

pairs.right: Orders this week per active user

questions.explain: Each better metric looks at real use now, not a big number that only grows.

questions.prompt: Why are rates often better than totals?
options: They show quality even as you grow
questions.explain: If users double but the 30 day return rate halves, the total hides a real problem. The rate shows it.

questions.prompt: Daily active users divided by monthly active users shows how often people come back.
questions.explain: This 'DAU/MAU' ratio is a stickiness check. WhatsApp is very high because people use it every day.

questions.prompt: Put these from least to most useful for judging a new feature.
steps: Number of people who saw it
Number who used it again next week
questions.explain: Repeat use is the strongest sign a feature is truly valuable.

lessons.title: Retention: do users come back?
teach: Retention is the share of users who come back after some time, like after 1 day, 7 days or 30 days.
If retention keeps falling to zero, the product has a leaky bucket: you keep pouring in users and they leak out.
Great products have a retention curve that falls at first and then flattens. The flat part is the group who found real value.

questions.prompt: 100 users join in May. 25 are still active in June. What is month 1 retention?
questions.explain: 25 out of 100 came back, so 25%.

questions.prompt: A retention curve that flattens is a good sign.
questions.explain: It means a core group keeps using the product. That's a sign of product market fit.

questions.prompt: Which idea does not help retention?
lines: A reminder at the time users usually order
Saving the last order for a one tap repeat
Spending more on ads for new users
A streak that rewards daily use
questions.explain: Ads bring new users. They don't make existing users come back.

questions.prompt: Match each product to what keeps users coming back.

pairs.right: Daily payments to shops and friends

questions.explain: Each has a reason to return: a habit, people you care about, money saved, or a daily need.

questions.prompt: A PM sees users leave after day 1. Where should they look first?
options: The first time experience: signup and first use
questions.explain: Day 1 drop off usually means users didn't reach value fast enough. Fix the first experience.

questions.prompt: Put these retention checks in time order.
questions.explain: Track users over time to see where the curve flattens.

questions.prompt: Growing sign ups fast can hide a retention problem.
questions.explain: Active users can look fine while most new users leave. Always look at retention by joining month, called cohorts.

lessons.title: Guardrails and trade-offs
teach: When you push one number, others can break. Guardrail metrics are the ones you promise not to hurt.
Faster delivery can mean more wrong items. More notifications can mean more uninstalls. Always pair a goal with a guardrail.
Good teams write their guardrails before they start an experiment, not after.

questions.prompt: Match each goal to a sensible guardrail.
questions.explain: Each guardrail catches the most likely harm from chasing the goal.

questions.prompt: Guardrails should be decided before the experiment starts.
questions.explain: If you pick them after, it's easy to ignore the bad news. Decide upfront what counts as harm.

questions.prompt: YouTube pushes watch time. Which guardrail makes most sense?
options: User satisfaction surveys and reports of harmful content
questions.explain: Watch time can rise from clickbait. Satisfaction and safety checks stop the team from winning the wrong way.

questions.prompt: Which line is not a guardrail for a ride app pushing more trips?
questions.explain: Number of rides is the goal itself. Guardrails watch what could go wrong while you chase it.

questions.prompt: Swiggy wants more orders from discounts. Pick the 3 guardrails.
questions.explain: Watch money lost per order, whether users still order without a coupon, and food quality.

questions.prompt: An experiment raises sign ups by 10% but doubles complaints. What now?
options: Ship it, sign ups are the goal
Hold it, find out why complaints rose
questions.explain: A broken guardrail is a warning. Understand the harm before you ship.

questions.prompt: Put these experiment steps in order.
steps: Run the test on some users
Check goal and guardrails, then decide
questions.explain: Goal and guardrails come first, then the test, then a decision using both.
